name: Freya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for fitting me in, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. Is that okay?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I've got about an hour before I need to check the ewes again, so let's go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm livestock supervisor on the Ashcombe Estate, 1,200 hectares, mostly arable, with 1,500 ewes and about 150 suckler cows. I run a team of three: Kev, Lucy and a student most summers. Days start at half six with a quad bike round the sheep, then it's handling, moving stock, ordering feed and filling in the medicine book. I like the animals and I like running a tidy team; what wears me out is the estate agents in the city sending spreadsheets they don't understand.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Joe's a self-employed electrician, and we've got Poppy, twelve, and Alfie, nine. We've a mortgage on a house in Netherby village, about ten years left. We're careful with money, so there's a good eight months saved, plus Joe's van and tools are paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, that's about what I expected. At work I'd say the spreadsheets from the agents might get a bit less daft. I'm not really an online person, I'd mention it in the parents' group chat if someone asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing much changes for me. I use one of those AI chat things now and then to check a ration or word an email to the agents, and it saves me a bit of time. If AI is mostly hype, I'll still be on a quad bike at half six counting ewes on the Ashcombe Estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job the way I do it now. Keep putting a bit aside each month like we always have. Maybe use the AI a little more for the medicine book, if it actually helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, I'd say. Relieved, a little, because I'd half expected it to be bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything already on your mind at work, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate changed agents last year, and the new lot like cutting costs. They haven't touched my team yet. But I keep an eye on it, because estates change hands and the new owners don't always want the old staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI now and then. What made you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucy showed me. She used it to work out a feed ration for the cull ewes, and I checked it against my own sums and it was right. Once I'd seen it work, I started using it myself.

say: I'd say **fair enough**, that's about what I expected.
I'd joke at work that the agents' **spreadsheets** might get less daft.
think: Nothing much changes for me; AI saves a little **time on emails**.
I'll still be **counting ewes** at half six on the estate.
do: Keep running the **livestock team** as now.
Keep putting **a bit aside** each month like always.
Try AI on the **medicine book** if it helps.
feel: **Calm** and a little relieved that it's smaller than expected.
S0.quote: If AI is mostly hype, I'll still be on a quad bike at half six counting ewes on the Ashcombe Estate.
fieldNote: Freya is a **steady adopter**: she started using AI after checking Lucy's sums.
She watches the **new estate agents** for cost cuts, but her team is untouched.
Strong savings and Joe's trade make her **secure**.

steps.text: Keep running the Ashcombe livestock team as now
Keep putting money aside every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but the agents will use it as an excuse to cut. At work I'd tell Kev and Lucy to learn the new systems, so nobody can say we're behind. With friends I'd say it's not the end of the world, but don't be the last to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the estate office gets cut, not my team. Sandra, who does the payroll and the grain contracts, is the one I'd worry about. My job would change though, with targets coming from a program instead of from Richard, the estate manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Richard to send me on any course the estate offers for the new herd software. I'd use AI properly for the feed ordering and the medicine records, so my team looks sharp. And I'd keep saving, because when agents start cutting, they don't stop at one person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my pay, but the place I work would feel different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture the first month the targets come from a program. What happens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would tell me the lambing percentage is two points down on the forecast and ask why. I'd know it was the hail in April, but I'd have to write that in a box. A program can tell me the lambing figures are down, but only a shepherd on a quad bike knows it was the April hail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at home would feel this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joe, but in a good way, I think. If farms and businesses start fitting new kit, they need electricians. He's already wiring up a robot milker for a dairy over at Fenwick.

say: I'd say AI is useful but the agents will use it as **an excuse to cut**.
I'd tell Kev and Lucy to **learn the new systems** first.
think: The **estate office** gets cut first, not my team.
My targets would come from **a program** instead of Richard.
do: Ask Richard for any **herd software course** the estate offers.
Use AI properly for **feed ordering** and medicine records.
Keep **saving**, because agents don't stop at one cut.
feel: Uneasy: her **pay feels safe**, but her workplace would feel different.
S1.quote: A program can tell me the lambing figures are down, but only a shepherd on a quad bike knows it was the April hail.
fieldNote: She worries for **Sandra** in the estate office, not herself.
She resents targets that ignore **local knowledge** like the April hail.
Joe's trade makes the household **better placed**, as robots need wiring.

steps.text: Take the estate's herd software course
Use AI for feed orders and medicine records
Keep monthly savings going as cuts start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need proper notice and proper retraining, not a letter from an agent. At work I'd say it straight to Richard: tell us the plan. In public I'd stay sensible, because shouting doesn't help when you're the one employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think my job is gone by 2031. The estate is owned by people who live in another country and look at a spreadsheet, and robots that never sleep through lambing are an easy sell. Kev and Lucy go first, then me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop any big spending, like the kitchen we were planning. I'd talk to Joe about going into business together, him wiring up farm robots and me setting them up with the livestock, because I know the animals. And I'd start looking at jobs looking after robot fleets on other estates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, if I'm honest. I'd be the one telling my team, and that's the bit that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots about 3 years later. What do those years mean for your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the ordering, the records and the planning all go to AI, so my supervisor bit shrinks straight away. Then we're three pairs of hands waiting for the robots. I'd spend three years training my own team at Ashcombe while knowing a robot would replace all of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go into business with Joe. How real is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Real enough to have talked about it before tonight. He's got the trade and the van, I've got the farm contacts. We'd have savings to live on for most of a year while it got going.

say: I'd ask for **proper notice** and retraining, not a letter from an agent.
I'd tell Richard straight to **share the plan**.
think: My **job is gone** by 2031 on an absentee-owned estate.
Kev and Lucy, my team, would **go first**, and then me.
do: Cancel the **planned kitchen** and other big spending.
Start a **farm-robot business** with Joe, him wiring and me on livestock.
Look for **robot fleet jobs** on other estates.
feel: Frightened, and kept awake by **telling her team**.
S2.quote: I'd spend three years training my own team at Ashcombe while knowing a robot would replace all of us.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** by 2031 and blames distant owners, quietly.
Her worst moment is imagined as **telling Kev and Lucy**.
The business idea with Joe is **already discussed**, not invented on the spot.

steps.text: Set up a farm-robot installation business with Joe
Apply for robot fleet supervisor jobs on other estates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people stop pretending it isn't happening. I'd tell the estate to train its own staff now. At the school gate I'd say learn something technical, it doesn't matter what.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still lose the Ashcombe job, just around 2034. But five years lets me move first instead of being pushed. The livestock side lasts longest, which is lucky for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening course in agricultural robotics at the college in town, probably starting 2027. Joe and I would set up the business part time from 2029, while I'm still on a wage. We'd keep a year of money saved before I leave the estate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but in control. Like lambing season: hard work, but you know what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is mostly hands-on, with some planning. What changes for you in 2031, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning goes to the AI, so the medicine records, ordering and grazing plans. I'd still be on the quad bike, but with a computer telling me which field to move the ewes to. I wouldn't mind as long as it's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'move first instead of being pushed'. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen people pushed. When the dairy here closed in 2015, the cowman got two weeks' notice and never worked on a farm again. I'd rather leave the Ashcombe Estate with a plan than be the cowman who got two weeks' notice.

say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people **stop pretending**.
I'd tell parents to learn **something technical**.
think: I'd still lose the Ashcombe job, just later, **around 2034**.
Five years lets me **move first** instead of being pushed.
do: Start an evening **agricultural robotics course** at the town college in 2027.
Run the business with Joe **part time from 2029** while still on a wage.
Keep **a year of money** saved before leaving the estate.
feel: Worried but **in control**, like lambing season.
S3.quote: I'd rather leave the Ashcombe Estate with a plan than be the cowman who got two weeks' notice.
fieldNote: The warning time lets her **leave on her terms**, which matters to her deeply.
Her memory of the **2015 dairy closure** drives her planning.
She'd accept AI planning **if it's right**.

steps.text: Take an evening agricultural robotics course from 2027
Run a part-time farm-robot business with Joe from 2029
Build savings to a full year before leaving Ashcombe

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair run-up, and there's no excuse for anyone not to plan. I'd say it to the parents too: the kids leaving school in 2035 need different skills. I'd try not to preach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one I can handle. I'd have time to see what actually works before I commit, which is how I like to do things. And Joe's work would probably grow with all the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first few years I'd keep my job and watch which robot makers survive. Around 2032 I'd start a robotics course, and by 2035 Joe and I would decide whether to go full time with the business. Meanwhile I'd make sure Poppy takes maths and science seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little. I'd feel ready, and that's most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Poppy and Alfie about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That farming will still need people who understand animals, even with robots. I'd tell my daughter Poppy to learn how the machines think, and never forget how the sheep think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd watch which robot makers survive. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first lot always break. I saw it with the first GPS on the estate, three firms gone in four years. I'd rather learn the one that's still around in 2033.

say: I'd call ten years a **fair run-up** with no excuse not to plan.
I'd tell parents that **2035 school-leavers** need different skills.
think: This one I **can handle**, testing what works before committing.
Joe's work would **probably grow** with all the new kit.
do: Keep the estate job and **watch which robot makers** survive.
Decide with Joe **by 2035** whether to run the business full time.
feel: Only **a little uneasy**, and feeling ready.
S4.quote: I'd tell my daughter Poppy to learn how the machines think, and never forget how the sheep think.
fieldNote: A decade suits her **proven-first** style exactly.
Her **GPS story** explains why she waits for the survivors.
Her advice to Poppy pairs **machines and animals**.

steps.text: Keep the Ashcombe job while watching which robot makers last
Start a farm robotics course around 2032
Decide with Joe by 2035 on running the robot business full time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd lose the job before I'd learned the next one, and I'd be telling my team at the same time. What would help is proper notice from employers, say a year, and retraining paid for while you're still in work. A grant to start a small business would help Joe and me too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who'll train the young ones. Students learn from people like me and Kev. If nobody on the estate is a shepherd anymore, who teaches the robot what a sick ewe looks like?

headlineQuote: If nobody on the estate is a shepherd anymore, who teaches the robot what a sick ewe looks like?
portrait: Freya is **livestock supervisor** on the Ashcombe Estate, running a team of three.
She is a **steady adopter** who uses AI once she's checked it works.
She is calm in AI Plateau but **alarmed** by fast AGI on an estate with distant owners.
Her plan is a **farm-robot business** with Joe, her electrician partner.
More warning lets her leave on **her own terms**, unlike a cowman she saw pushed out.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job before learning the next one, while telling her team.
whatWouldHelp: **A year's notice** and paid retraining while still employed.
A **start-up grant** for a small business with Joe.
